The short version

Fusion magnets depend on mines that today's laws barely reach

We checked 13 rules against 4 mining regions that supply the yttrium, tin and niobium inside fusion superconducting magnets. Only 4 of the 52 checks find a rule that fully applies.

Why it matters

Stronger magnets, harder questions

Why the magnets matter

Superconducting magnets carry huge currents with no electrical resistance when cooled, so they can make fields of 10 to 20 tesla. The stronger the field, the smaller a reactor can be for the same power. That is a big reason companies are now attempting compact fusion with new tape-based magnets.

power density vs ITER
radius for the same power
Rough rule of thumb: fusion power density rises with the fourth power of field strength when other plasma conditions are held equal. Real designs differ.

Why sourcing matters

Every one of these coils depends on a few elements, and some of them come from places with documented abuse.

⛓
Clean energy, harmful inputsYttrium, tin and niobium are traced to mines with forced labor, child labor, armed-group financing and toxic pollution.
⚖
The law mostly misses itOnly 4 of 52 rule checks fully apply today. Duties stop at raw-ore importers, so buyers of finished tape and wire are rarely asked anything.
✦
Cheap to fix nowFusion buys tiny volumes, and much of it is publicly funded. A sourcing condition on that money costs little and reaches nearly every magnet maker while supply chains are still small.

Data, methods and sources

How this was built

The dataset behind every chart, how each verdict was decided, and where the evidence comes from. Rule terms checked 9 November 2026.

1The dataset

The core dataset is a rule-by-region matrix: 13 rules assessed against 4 mining regions, giving 52 cells. Each cell records whether a rule reaches the harm documented in that region, and what slips through if it doesn't.

Regions4Kachin State, Myanmar · Shan State and Wa, Myanmar · Bangka Belitung, Indonesia · Rubaya, North Kivu, DR Congo (traded through Rwanda)
Minerals5Yttrium and heavy rare earths · other rare earths · tin · niobium · tantalum

2Methods

2.1 Choosing regions

A region is included only if it meets all three tests:

  1. It produces a mineral used in fusion superconducting magnets: rare earths for REBCO tape, or tin and niobium for Nb₃Sn and NbTi wire.
  2. Credible reporting from NGOs, the UN, major news outlets or governments documents serious harm there: forced or child labor, armed-group financing, or major environmental damage.
  3. The mineral leaves the region through a route where its origin can be lost, such as separation, smelting or re-export through a third country.

The four regions illustrate how the rules fail. They are not a full survey of fusion's mineral supply. Brazil, which supplies about 90% of the world's niobium, and lower-risk rare earth sources are deliberately left out.

2.2 Choosing rules

A rule is included if it could plausibly reach at least one region through a mineral list, a type of harm (forced labor, human rights or environmental harm), a geographic program or a trade control. The set mixes binding law, voluntary standards and non-legal levers such as sanctions, export licensing and local enforcement, because readers choose among all of them.

2.3 Deciding a verdict

Each cell is scored by asking four questions in order. The first answer that settles it decides the verdict.

One extra check applies to fusion supply chains: does the duty sit where fusion buyers actually purchase (finished tape, wire or magnets), or only with the importer of raw ore? Several "Partly reaches" verdicts come from this check.

2.4 Writing the gap

Each gap statement says what happens in practice: who can buy what without being asked about it. Statements stay within what the rule text and the cited reporting support. When a rule fits on paper but is hard to enforce, as with §307 when origin is lost during separation in China, the difficulty is written into the gap rather than used to lower the verdict.

2.5 Checking rule terms

Scopes, thresholds and dates were checked against the cited sources on 9 November 2026. Three rules were changing on that date and should be re-checked before anyone cites them: Dodd-Frank §1502 (future uncertain), Germany's LkSG (amendment before the Bundestag) and the EU Battery Regulation (narrower scope under negotiation).

2.6 Tally check

The verdict counts below were recounted from the matrix rows. All four match the coverage tallies in the research document.

    4.5 Reactor and magnet facts

    • ITER: Magnets: 18 D-shaped toroidal field coils, six ring-shaped poloidal field coils, a central solenoid of six modules, and Nb₃Sn and NbTi conductors cooled to about 4 K (−269 °C).
    • ITER: What is fusion?: plasma at 150 million °C, about ten times hotter than the Sun's core.
    • MIT News (Sep 2021): the 20-tesla high-temperature superconducting magnet built by CFS and MIT.
    • Commonwealth Fusion Systems, Tokamak Energy and Proxima Fusion: each describes its high-temperature superconducting magnets.
    • Rare-earth barium copper oxide and an IPAC'10 paper: REBCO tape can be made with yttrium or gadolinium.

    Evidence to strengthen before publication

    IssueWhereSuggested fix

    Corrections from the source check (9 November 2026)

    Every documented-harm figure on this site was checked against a primary or major source. These items in the original research did not hold up and were changed:

    • Shan and Wa: "rare earth sites rose from 12 to 85 after the coup" could not be traced to any source. It was replaced with the satellite count of 63 sites near the Chinese border (Shan Human Rights Foundation and Stimson Center, via Yale Environment 360).
    • Shan and Wa: pollution of the Salween River is not documented, because the river is not monitored. The documented case is the Kok River, with about $40 million in losses downstream in Thailand.
    • Bangka Belitung: "240,000 hectares of mangrove damaged" could not be traced to a primary source; Walhi has reported 400 hectares. It was replaced with the September 2025 crackdown on 1,000 illegal mines.
    • Bangka Belitung: the 57 deaths in abandoned pits (JATAM, 2014–2020) are not broken down by age. "Mostly children" applies to the national total of 168.
    • Rubaya: "child labor is common" had no strong source. It was replaced with the two 2026 mine collapses reported by Reuters.
    • Kachin: toxic waste in the N'Mai Kha is described by Global Witness as a fear of residents, not a measured finding. The tile now uses Stimson Center mine counts.
    • Weaker sources removed: a Wikipedia mirror (replaced by the ILO survey), Karen News, BNI and an AP article republished by Africanews.

    Consistency notes

    • UFLPA in Bangka Belitung and Rubaya is scored "Doesn't reach," but its gap text says the rule is not relevant. Under the verdict steps in 2.3, it would score "Not relevant." It is kept as "Doesn't reach" to show that the strongest US import tool is limited to one geography. One approach should be chosen and applied to every region.
    • The EU Battery Regulation is scored "Doesn't reach" in every region, which is consistent: it is ruled out by mineral, not by lack of a link.

    Scope limits

    • The matrix measures whether a rule reaches a harm on paper. It does not measure how strongly the rule is enforced, except where the gap text says so.
    • It covers four high-risk regions with documented harm. It does not estimate how much fusion magnet material comes from them.
    • Rule terms are as of 9 November 2026, and several rules are changing.
    • This is research, not legal advice.

    6Keeping it current

    1. Re-check each rule's status against its sources, starting with the three that are changing (see 2.5).
    2. Re-run the verdict steps (2.3) for any rule whose scope or start date has changed.
    3. Recount the tallies (2.6).
    4. Update the "checked" date on the site and in the research documents.
